interaction in Eq. (2) and later, are the electron operators defined for one particular spin
and valley? It is difficult to find in the paper whether the pairing is intra-valley or
intervalley. Also, I don’t think k_{F,1} and k_{F,2} are defined before they first appear.
Our response: We apologize for the confusion. In the revised version, we have clarified
below Eq. (2) that the electron operators are for spin-polarized electrons within a single
valley. To further clarify that the pairing is intra-valley, we added a specification in the
summarizing paragraph at the end of our introduction. We further clarified that k_F1
and k_F2 are the momenta of the inner and outer Fermi surfaces, respectively, in the
caption of Fig 1 where they first appear.
Reviewer #4: 5. The effective attractive interaction near r=1nm in Fig. 2(c) is
counterintuitive. RPA, which can be understood as the dynamical generalization of
Thomas-Fermi screening, usually only reduces the repulsion due to opposite charges
accumulated nearby. It seems unlikely to have “over-screening” that the repulsion is
flipped into attractions. It is more likely that the interaction is attractive in non-s wave
channels, instead of being globally attractive. Although s-wave here is forbidden by
spin-valley polarization, the RPA calculations seem to be independent from this
assumption. Can the authors provide an intuitive picture for understanding the
attraction? Also, RPA is a perturbative method for interactions much smaller than the
Fermi energy, how is it justified here, where interaction is much larger than the kinetic
energy (as indicated by r_s the authors calculated)?
Our response: It is correct that the RPA calculations are independent from any
assumptions on the pairing symmetry. Indeed, we find that the RPA screened potential
becomes attractive on a length scale of a fraction of the Fermi wavelength. Intuitively,
this arises from Friedel oscillations of the electrostatic potential of a charge placed in
an electron gas: In the presence of strong screening, the strong repulsion of the bare
Coulomb interaction is sufficiently suppressed so that Friedel oscillations become
larger than the screened Coulomb repulsion, leading to an effective attraction.
Independent of spin-polarization, this screened potential generally favors finite angular
momentum pairing over s-wave, because a strong repulsion at very short distances
remains.
The RPA calculation here is only expected to be only qualitatively correct, because it’s
quantitative accuracy is not justified for strong interactions as the Referee points out. It
is well-known that RPA tends to overestimate pairing strength, see also our response
to comment 1 of Referee #2. However, it has been argued that RPA captures the
qualitatively correct features, see for example Ref. [X. Can et al., PRB 106, L220502
(2022)].
We clarified in the main text:
“In real space, the screening strongly reduces the repulsion above the Thomas-Fermi
screening length $\ell_{\rm TF}$. Furthermore, Friedel oscillations appear with period
$2 k_{F,1},\ 2 k_{F,2}$ due to the two Fermi surfaces. When the Thomas-Fermi
screening length is much shorter than the wavelengths $\pi/k_{F,1},\ \pi/k_{F,2}$,
Friedel oscillations dominate over Coulomb repulsion and lead to an effective attraction
at short length scales, as obtained from our calculations shown in Fig.\ref{fig:2}(c). We
find $\ell_{\rm TF} \approx 1$ to $2\ {\rm nm}$, for typical parameters where we
observe superconductivity as discussed below, while $2\pi/k_{F}$ is typically around
$20 \ {\rm nm} $ to $ 30\ {\rm nm}$. This mechanism benefits from a mexican-hat
shaped dispersion because the additional pocket contributes a large density of states
leading to a short Thomas-Fermi screening length. This enables superconductivity at
larger density.”
Reviewer #4: 6. A related question, is the effective RPA interaction above sufficient to
induce spin-valley polarization, i.e., the starting point of the current theory? The
interaction in Fig. 2(c) looks much weaker and localized than the bare interaction; the
highly local interaction may resemble the Hubbard model which gives anti-
ferromagnetism instead of (orbital) ferromagnetism.
Our response: It is correct that isospin polarization and superconductivity both occur
from Coulomb repulsion. However, they occur at different energy scales, and we treat
superconducting order perturbatively with respect to the isospin order. Isospin
polarization can be obtained in a Stoner model where the energy scale is \nu(E_F) V(2
k_F) E_F \approx 2 meV where \nu(E_F) is the density of states at the Fermi energy E_F
and V(2 k_F) is a measure for the bare Coulomb interaction energy at the (outer) Fermi
surface. This energy scale is about an order of magnitude larger than the pairing
strength (compare to manuscript Fig. 4). A detailed discussion on how the isospin
polarization is obtained from the Stoner model applied to rhombohedral graphene is
contained in Ref. Ghazaryan et al., PRB 2023.
Please see also our response to Referee 1, comment 2.
Reviewer #4: 7. The form factor or the interaction in Eq. (13) looks incorrect.
Shouldn’t it be the inner product of u_{k+q} with u_k, and u_{k’-q} with u_{k’}?
Our response: We thank the Referee for the careful reading and correcting the typo.
Reviewer #4: 8. I do not understand what “charge-ordered state” in the discussion
mean. Does it mean Wigner Crystal? The authors may want to clarify. Also, there is
(almost) no mentioning of the Lifshitz transition of Fermi surface in the main text
(probably the cyan line region in Fig. 4?), which the authors should explain better.
Our response: By charge-ordered state, we imply the general class of states with a
charge-density order. This includes charge-density waves and Wigner crystals. These
two charge orders are continuously connected as the Wigner crystal is the extreme
limit of a charge density wave where the magnitude of the wave approaches the mean
electron density, so that the charge density in the valleys of the wave approaches zero.
We further thank the referee for the suggestion to clarify the Lifshitz transition in our
manuscript. At the first mentioning of the Lifshitz transition in the main text, we now
clarify:
“In this case, a Lifshitz transition from simply-connected to annular Fermi sea occurs
when the Fermi energy crosses the top of the hat as the electron density is reduced.”
The Lifshitz transition is depicted by the white dashed line in our numerical results of
Fig. 3(a), 3(b), and 4(b). We now emphasize this fact in the caption of both figures.
The cyan-shaded region encircled by the cyan line in Fig 4(b) marks the region where
the gas parameter r_s is larger than 40. Qualitatively, a large gas parameter indicates
that the system may likely charge-order into a Wigner crystalline, insulating state. We
comment on this region in section “Competing state” on page 5 of our manuscript.
Reviewer #4: 9. The electron-phonon coupling is completely ignored in the study here.
Is there a particular reason for ignoring the effect of phonons? Also, how would the
authors propose to tell experimentally whether the superconductivity is from Coulomb
repulsion instead of phonons? For instance, if the screening of Coulomb interaction is
enhanced (by metallic gate, etc), would the authors predict an enhancement or
decrease of superconducting Tc?
Our response: We thank the Referee for the suggestion of investigating the role of
phonons and how to tell whether the mechanism is from charge fluctuations by
screening.
Regarding phonons, we included the following text in the discussion section (see also
our response to Referee 2, comment (4)):
“Alternative mechanisms for superconductivity in an isospin-polarized metal include
phonons and fluctuations of the isospin polarization. We assume that the
superconductivity develops on top of a fully spin- and valley-polarized state, which is in
line with experimental observation. For such case, the Pauli principle requires the
superconducting state to be odd-parity. However, phonons typically lead to an
isotropic attraction that favors the $s$-wave channel and is averaged out for higher
angular momenta, and thus, we expect that this is likely not an important mechanism
for pairing for the system considered here. Fluctuations of the isospin order parameter
can indeed mediate strong pairing in the proximity to the phase transition in the isospin
order \cite{Fay1980Oct,Lohneysen2007Aug,Dong2023May,Dong2023Oct}. We remark
that these fluctuations are not present in the fully polarized phase that we consider
here.”
Regarding the effect of screening from gates, we found that it only plays role when the
distance to the metallic gates is on order of the Thomas-Fermi screening length. The
Thomas-Fermi screening length in the superconducting regions is on order of 1-2 nm.
When reducing the gate distance to this length scale, the superconducting pairing and
the transition temperature are indeed reduced. This is detailed in our new Appendix F.
Additionally, we comment in the discussion section:
“We note that, besides possible suppression of a charge-ordered competing state,
screening from metallic gates becomes relevant to the superconducting state only
when the distance to the metallic gates becomes of order of $\ell_{\rm TF}$. Because
typical distances to metallic fields in experiment are of order $30\ {\rm nm}$, much
larger than the typical $\ell_{\rm TF} \approx 1$ to $2 \ {\rm nm}$ obtained from our
calculations, gate-screening is irrelavant to the superconducting state. Only when
reducing the gate distance to the order of $\ell_{\rm TF}$ the superconducting order
gets suppressed, see App.\ref{app:gate_screening} for details. ”
Reviewer #4: 10. The authors only focused on the time-reversal breaking
superconducting phases in the experiment. The experiment also observes more
conventional superconductivity in two other parameter regimes. Do the authors have
comments on the other superconductivity regimes? Is the claim that Coulomb
interaction is better for realizing chiral superconductivity (in contrast to phonons which
may favor s-wave superconductivity more)?
Our response: Thank you for your question. At this point, we prefer to keep the focus
of our manuscript on the novel time-reversal symmetry breaking phases and leave a
unifying discussion of the full phase diagram for future work.

already.
Our response: We thank the Referee for pointing to this typo and corrected it.

density variations are on atomistic length scales. Detecting these in tunneling
spectroscopy would require atomic-resolution STM measurements, which are
inaccessible because the sample is enclosed on both sides with hBN and graphite
gates.
It may be possible to detect signatures of the finite momentum pairing in Josephson
coupling experiments such as proposed in [Phys. Rev. Lett. 84, 4970], or in
side-contacted tunneling conductance measurements [Sci. Adv.10, eadr4817 (2024)].

First, the original experiment (posted before the original submission of this work) has reported an insulating state separating SC1 and SC2. Second, the authors did not do any concrete calculations related to the Wigner crystal. Wigner crystal is a nice suggestion/speculation but not a concrete prediction by the authors. (4) Regarding Reviewer #1's point 1: The authors' response is based on the density of states, which affects the Thomas-Fermi screening length. You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

A microscopic mechanism for chiral p-wave superconductivity from Coulomb repulsion is proposed for spin- and valley-polarized state of rhombohedral multilayer graphene. The superconducting instability arises when strong Thomas-Fermi screening of the Coulomb potential allows Friedel oscillations to take over–leading to an effective attraction on length scales below the Fermi wavelength. The superconducting critical temperature is largest at low density below a Lifshitz transition to an annular Fermi sea, where the additional pocket strongly enhances Thomas-Fermi screening. The Lifshitz transition also marks a topological phase transition from a trivial to a topological superconducting phase hosting Majorana fermions. The chirality of the superconducting order parameter is selected by the chirality of the valley-polarized Bloch electrons. Our results are in reasonable agreement with observations in a recent experiment on tetralayer graphene.

---

## Introduction

Chiral superconductivity, characterized by spontaneous time-reversal symmetry breaking and finite-angular momentum Cooper pairing1, is a long-sought quantum phase of matter with unusual superconducting and magnetic properties. Interest in chiral superconductors is further fueled by their potential for hosting topological phases and Majorana fermions2,3. While previous material candidates, such as Sr2RuO4 and UTe25–7, showed initial signs of chiral superconductivity, recent experiments strongly suggest single-component superconducting order parameters that are non-chiral8–15.

Very recently, signatures of chiral superconductivity have been observed in rhombohedral-stacked tetralayer graphene under electron doping16. While superconductivity has been previously discovered and intensively studied in crystalline trilayer17–30 and bilayer graphene31–36, the newly found superconducting state in tetralayer graphene at low density is remarkably distinctive in that it exhibits large spontaneous anomalous Hall effect above Tc and magnetic hysteresis in resistance below Tc. These observations demonstrate time-reversal-breaking superconductivity in a pure carbon system. Its pairing symmetry and pairing mechanism are open questions for investigation.

A key feature of rhombohedral multilayer graphene is the flat band dispersion near K and K0 point, leading to a strong correlation effect19,23. As a result, spin and valley isospin symmetry breaking occurs at low temperature, giving rise to half and quarter metal phases23. Interestingly, the superconducting state in tetralayer graphene at low density borders the quarter metal and its phase boundary shows no or little change with the applied magnetic field, indicating that the superconducting state is likely fully spin and valley polarized16. Thus, tetralayer graphene provides a rare opportunity for investigating Cooper pairing of single-flavor electrons in a solid-state platform.

In this work, we study the microscopic mechanism and pairing symmetry of superconductivity in multilayer graphene that develops from the spin- and valley-polarized quarter metal normal state [Fig. 1a, b]. Our mechanism is based on the overscreening of Coulomb interaction due to charge fluctuations, which leads to an effective attraction at length scales on a fraction of the Fermi wavelength, driving Cooper pairing. Using a minimal model for the band dispersion, our theory predicts that superconductivity occurs at low densities with enhanced density of states due to the annular Fermi surface and displacement field-induced flatness of the band. Based on our analysis, we further propose that a Wigner crystalline insulating state occurs at the Lifshitz transition from simply-connected to annular Fermi sea that splits the superconducting dome into two. This provides an explanation for the two proximate superconducting domes SC1 and SC2 with similar properties observed in the experiment16.

---

## Results

Band dispersion
In rhombohedral multilayer graphene, low-energy bands come from sublattice-polarized states in the top and bottom layers. An out-of-plane electric field induces a potential bias equal to 2D between these layers and opens up an energy gap while flattening the dispersion near K and K0 points. Therefore, the Fermi energy is only a few meV above the band bottom for a small electron density of around 5 × 1011 cm−2, where time-reversal-breaking superconductivity is observed.

The low-energy band dispersion is highly tunable by the electric field. As the displacement field D increases, the curvature at K and K0 changes from positive to negative19,23 as shown in Fig. 1c for ABCA tetralayer graphene, resulting in a Mexican-hat shaped dispersion. In this case, a Lifshitz transition from simply-connected to annular Fermi surface occurs when the Fermi energy crosses the top of the hat as the electron density is reduced.

We capture the essential features of the electric-field-tuned conduction band in rhombohedral n-layer graphene with a minimal band

εk = D 1 + (k/k0)2n + ℏ2k2 / 2m (1)

where D is the displacement field, k0 is a momentum scale, and m is the effective mass. The dispersion (1) is circularlysymmetric. The inclusion of additional hopping terms leads to trigonal warping. For now, we neglect trigonal warping and Berry curvature effects and will treat them perturbatively later.

Rytova-Keldysh potential
The density-density interaction can be written as

Hint = 1/2 sum_{k1,k2,q} V(q) ψ^y_{k1+q} ψ^y_{k2-q} ψ_{k2} ψ_{k1} (2)

where ψ^y_k (ψ_k) are the annihilation (creation) operators of spin-polarized electrons in a single valley. Importantly, in a 2D material surrounded by a dielectric with a lower dielectric permittivity, the Coulomb interaction between two charges can be described by the Rytova-Keldysh potential40–42, taking the form:

V(q) = e^2 / 2ϵ|q|(1 + rK|q|) (3)

where ϵ = 5ϵ0 is the dielectric permittivity of the surrounding hBN (with ϵ0 the vacuum permittivity), and rK is the Rytova-Keldysh parameter. The Rytova-Keldysh parameter depends on the difference between the dielectric response of the 2D material under study and that of the surrounding insulator. Since the 2D dielectric screening is determined by interband transitions and thereby depends on the band gap, rK of multilayer graphene is affected by the displacement field43. We will find that the superconducting pairing strength depends sensitively on rK.

Electron pairing from screened Coulomb repulsion
We study superconductivity in the spin- and valley-polarized state. This is justified because (i) valley polarization is observed to occur at a much higher temperature than superconductivity, and (ii) the primary superconducting state (SC1 in ref. 16) was observed within the quarter-metal state, and (iii) the primary superconducting states (SC1 and SC2) survive to very high in-plane magnetic fields.

Theoretically, we also expect that the energy scales of spin- and valley polarization to be much larger than superconductivity: Estimating the energy scale of isospin polarization in the Stoner model23 as Δpol ≈ ν(EF)V(2kF,2)EF ≈ 2 to 3 meV in the relevant range of density and displacement field, it is an order of magnitude larger than the pairing strength [see numerical results below].

Since total spin S2 and valley imbalance NK − NK0 are conserved quantum numbers, there are no isospin fluctuations at zero temperature that can drive superconductivity in the fully-polarized quarter metal state. This motivates us to consider a mechanism for superconductivity in the spin- and valley-polarized state based on screening of electron-electron interactions by charge fluctuations44–46. The screening is described by the charge susceptibility χRe(q,τ) = −1/A <T τ ρe,q(τ)ρe,-q(0)>, which in random phase approximation (RPA) is determined by the expression

χRe(q,iΩn)RPA = χ0e(q,iΩn) / 1 - Vq χ0e(q,iΩn) (4)

in terms of the charge susceptibility of the non-interacting electron gas

χ0e(q,iΩn) = 1/A sum_k (nF(εk) - nF(εk+q)) / (εk - εk+q + iℏΩn) (5)

where nF is the Fermi-Dirac distribution. The screened interaction potential is then

V~(q) = Vq / 1 - Vq χ0e(q,0) = Vq ϵ^-1(q,0)RPA (6)

The charge susceptibility and screened interaction potential for the annular Fermi pocket are shown in Fig. 2a, b, respectively. The q→0 limit of the denominator describing the screened interaction in Eq. (6) lim_{q→0} Vq χ0e(q,0) = e^2 / 2πℓTF defines the Thomas-Fermi screening length ℓTF = 4πϵ/e^2ν(EF).

Due to the large density of states, the charge susceptibility becomes large for momenta below twice the Fermi momentum kF,2 of the outer Fermi surface. This leads to a suppression of the electron-electron interaction at small momenta and a peak at 2kF,2. This renormalized interaction potential promotes a p-wave superconducting instability.

In real space, the screening strongly reduces the repulsion above the Thomas-Fermi screening length ℓTF. Furthermore, Friedel oscillations appear with period 2kF,1, 2kF,2 due to the two Fermi surfaces. When the Thomas-Fermi screening length is much shorter than the wavelengths π/kF,1, π/kF,2, Friedel oscillations dominate over Coulomb repulsion and lead to an effective attraction at short length scales, as obtained from our calculations shown in Fig. 2c. We find ℓTF ≈ 1 to 2 nm, for typical parameters where we observe superconductivity as discussed below, while 2π/kF,1, 2π/kF,2 is typically around 20 nm to 30 nm. This mechanism benefits from a Mexican-hat-shaped dispersion because the additional pocket contributes a large density of states, leading to a short Thomas-Fermi screening length. This enables superconductivity at a larger density.

To determine the superconducting order parameter and its critical temperature, we solve the self-consistency equations

Δ(k) = -1/A sum_{k'} V~(k-k') <ψ^y_{-k'} ψ^y_{k'}> (7)

<ψ^y_{-k} ψ^y_{k}> = - Δ(k) / 2Ek tanh(Ek / 2kBT)

where Ek is the quasiparticle energy

Ek = sqrt((εk - μ)^2 + |Δ(k)|^2) (8)

Here, the interaction V~(k-k') scatters a pair of electrons at opposite momenta (k', -k') to (k, -k).

Due to the rotational symmetry in our model, we decompose the pairing interaction into angular harmonics:

V~l(k,k') = 1/2π integral_0^{2π} dϑ e^{ilϑ} V~(ϑ,k,k') (9)

where we wrote V~(k-k') = V~(ϑ,k,k') with ϑ the angle between k and k', and k, k' the their magnitude. The order parameter can also be expanded into angular harmonics Δ(k) = sum_{l=0} ηl(k) e^{ilθ} with (kx, ky) = k(cosθ, sinθ). The equations for the critical temperature Tc for different angular harmonics decouple.

Around Tc, we linearize the self-consistency equation and find for the individual angular harmonics,

ηl(k,Tc) = - 1/8π^2 integral_0^∞ dk' k' V~l(k,k') tanh(|εk' - μ| / 2kBTc) / |εk' - μ| ηl(k',Tc) (10)

For the superconducting order parameter at zero temperature, the self-consistency relation reads

ηl(k,0) = - 1/8π^2 integral_0^∞ dk' k' V~l(k,k') ηl(k',0) / 2 sqrt((εk' - μ)^2 + |ηl(k',0)|^2) (11)

Both equations can be solved iteratively, as detailed in SM section B. This angular decomposition applies to a circularly symmetric interaction potential, where the circular symmetry is preserved for the screened potential when the dispersion is circularly symmetric.

Importantly, the screened interaction V~ is positive and large at momentum transfer q = k-k' around 2kF,2, compared to small q. Such q-dependent interaction favors an order parameter that takes opposite signs at opposite ±k points on the Fermi surface, i.e., it favors p-wave pairing.

For most superconductors, the pairing interaction is weak and therefore the pairing potential Δ(k) is small compared to the Fermi energy and only appreciable in the vicinity of the Fermi surface. For this reason, in solving the gap equation, it suffices to use “on-shell” pairing interaction V~l(k,k') at Fermi wave vectors k, k'. In contrast, in multilayer graphene, the combination of low electron density and flat band bottom leads to a larger ratio of interaction to the Fermi energy. As a consequence, we will show that Δ and Tc can be on the order of the Fermi energy. Indeed, the recent experiment on tetralayer graphene16 reports an unusually high upper critical field at low density, indicating a strong-coupling superconductor with coherence length comparable to interparticle distance. For strong-coupling superconductors, the superconducting gap Δ(k) can be large even away from the Fermi momentum. Therefore, in solving the gap equation, it is necessary to use the interaction V~l(k,k') with full k, k' dependence.

Our calculation of the density of states, ν and critical temperature Tc, as a function of electron density and displacement field, is shown in Fig. 3a, b, respectively. Both the displacement field D and the electron density n together determine the Fermi surface size and topology. For small D < Dc ≈ 40 meV, the dispersion increases monotonically with k and the Fermi surface is a single circle with kF = sqrt(4πn), whereas at large displacement field (D > Dc), a Lifshitz transition from annular to simply-connected Fermi sea occurs with increasing electron density, which is accompanied by a large jump in the normal-state density of states at the Fermi level [Fig. 3a]. Correspondingly, superconducting properties depend strongly on the displacement field. For small D, a superconducting state is found at a small density where the chemical potential lies close to the relatively flat band bottom with a large density of states. For large D, the superconducting state sets in at low densities where the Fermi sea is annular, and Tc is largest close to the Lifshitz transition.

It should be noted that the value of Tc is sensitive to the dielectric screening of Coulomb repulsion by the multilayer graphene, which, in turn, depends on the displacement field-induced band gap. As a function of the Rytova-Keldysh parameter rK [Fig. 3c], the typical Tc at D = 60 meV ranges from Tc ≈ 3 K at rK = 1 nm to a suppression of Tc to below 0.1 K above rK = 10 nm. With bare Coulomb repulsion, a maximal Tc ≈ 8 K is obtained, see SM section H. The decrease of Tc with strong dielectric screening is consistent with electron pairing by Coulomb repulsion. Without knowing the value of rK for tetralayer graphene, we cannot make a quantitative prediction of Tc. Nonetheless, for the reasonable range of rK considered here, superconductivity always onsets at n < 0.7 × 1012 cm−2 in agreement with experimental observation, and the calculated Tc is acceptable compared to the experimental value, especially considering that the mean-field theory generally predicts higher values of Tc.

Going beyond our mean-field treatment, we estimate the critical temperature for a BKT transition47–49 kBTBKT = π/2 J determined by the superfluid stiffness. An order-of-magnitude estimate is obtained using the superfluid stiffness expression J = ℏ^2n/4m for a quadratic band whose mass m ≈ 2me is matched so that its density of states matches the typical density of state ν(EF) ≈ 2νe at the Fermi energy of our model [compare Fig. 3a]. Based on this estimate, we find a typical BKT transition temperature kBTBKT ≈ 0.9 K at n = 0.5 × 1012 cm−2. This indicates that the critical temperature in this system may be limited by vortex proliferation in the BKT transition.

Strong-coupling superconductivity
For the chiral px ± ipy pairing, the calculated pairing potential Δ(k) at T = 0 can reach a few tenths of the Fermi energy. Notably, Δ(k) is large not only close to the Fermi surface, but also extends to several times the Fermi wavevector with a sign change at around 2kF,2 [Fig. 4a]. Its functional form closely follows the interaction potential up to a proportionality factor setting the pairing strength [see SM section C]. The presence of substantial pairing potential away from the Fermi surfaces is a consequence of the strong-coupling nature of this superconducting state—because kBTc and Δ are of the order of the Fermi energy, pairing between electrons away from the Fermi surface is relevant. This is captured by our direct solution of Eqs. (10), (11).

Due to the large pairing potential, the chemical potential changes appreciably in the superconducting state. This can be estimated by taking into account the pairing potential in relating electron density to chemical potential

n = 1/2πℏ^2 integral d^2k (1 - (εk - μ) / Ek) (12)

At zero temperature, the change in chemical potential approaches 0.1 meV. The change in electron density is taken into account in Fig. 3a. The change in chemical potential δμ ∝ |Δ|^2 is expected to increase linearly with decreasing temperature.

Topological superconductivity and Lifshitz transition
The quasiparticle gap Δ0 = min_k Ek as a function of density n and displacement field D is shown in Fig. 4b. Our p±ip superconductor generally has a full gap, except at the Lifshitz transition from simply-connected to annular Fermi sea, where the system has a point node at the Fermi point k = 0 at which the pairing potential vanishes. The closing of the quasiparticle gap marks a topological quantum phase transition from a topological superconductor with unity Chern number in the region with a single Fermi pocket to a topologically trivial state in the annular region at large displacement fields50,51. The topological superconductor at small displacement fields hosts chiral Majorana edge modes and Majorana zero modes in the vortex2. In contrast, the trivial state with annular Fermi sea is adiabatically connected to the Bose-Einstein limit μ → −∞, because the pairing potential Δ(k) is finite at the band bottom of the Mexican hat dispersion, which forms a ring at k ≠ 0. Note that in our theory, even though the superconducting gap vanishes at k = 0 at the Lifshitz transition, the gap at the outer Fermi surface Δ(kF2) and critical temperature remains large throughout the transition – therefore the quasiparticle gap closure is not visible in the critical temperature calculations Fig. 3b.

Competing state
Since the p-wave superconductivity found in our RPA calculation occurs at relatively low density, it is important to consider its competition with the Wigner crystal state, which generally appears in 2D Coulomb systems at sufficiently low density. To estimate the transition to the Wigner crystal, we compute the gas parameter rs = Eint/Ekin given by the ratio of interaction Eint to kinetic energy Ekin52. In our calculations, we find that the superconducting state is robust against the Wigner crystal state for rs < 40. The transition to the Wigner crystal depends sensitively on the gate screening as the interparticle distances at low density approach tens of nm.

In Fig. 4, the region where rs > 40 is encircled by the cyan line; in a homogeneous electron gas, the transition to a Wigner crystal occurs around rs ≈ 30–4052–56. This region is where the band bottom is most flat, so that the kinetic energy per particle is low. It coincides with the region where the density of states is largest, see Fig. 3a. We expect crystalline order is likely to dominate there, so that the superconducting region is divided into two, separated by an insulating Wigner crystal state.

Trigonal warping and Berry curvature effects
Our minimal model neglects trigonal warping, which arises from electron hoppings beyond nearest-neighbor atoms in multilayer graphene. With trigonal warping, the band dispersion becomes asymmetric εk ≠ ε-k, which weakens intravalley pairing between ±k states. Fortunately, the energy scale of trigonal warping is small in tetralayer graphene in the range of density and displacement field of interest, as evidenced by the nearly symmetric band dispersion in Fig. 1. For the range of parameters where we observe superconductivity, the pairing is driven by the interaction energy, and therefore is robust against the pair breaking effect of trigonal warping.

Up to now, we have neglected the effect of electron Bloch wave functions |uk> within the unit cell. The momentum dependence of the complex-valued wavefunction |uk> gives rise to Berry curvature, which in the presence of time-reversal symmetry breaking, leads to an orbital magnetic moment in the polarized valley57. We have shown that the chirality of the Bloch wave functions is responsible for the chirality of the superconducting order parameter. We also verified that our mechanism strongly favors p-wave pairing over higher angular momenta, see SM section G.

### Reviewer 1

In this paper, the authors propose chiral p-wave superconductivity in tetralayer graphene. Considering a quarter metal state with a nearly flat band, they obtain a chiral p-wave superconducting state from the screened Coulomb interaction. They also find the Fermi surface of the system shows the Lifshitz transition, which results in a topological phase transition. The topic is timely, and the result is interesting. However, the following points need to be clarified before making a recommendation, as they are crucial for understanding and accepting the research.
1. The authors only consider a particular multilayer graphene, ABCA tetralayer graphene. The author should clarify why they chose this specific multilayer graphene. For example, is it possible to obtain a similar result in trilayer graphene or differently stacked graphene
2. The authors assume a spin and magnetic gap deriving the quarter metal, then calculate the superconducting critical temperature independently from a screened Coulomb interaction. However, the magnetic order itself also originates from the Coulomb interaction. The author should justify this treatment.
3. A minor point: When D is introduced in the left column on page 2 for the first time, the author should explicitly mention its definition because 2D is often used to represent “two dimensions.”

### Reviewer 2

The authors proposed that the screened Coulomb interaction can realize chiral superconductivity in rhombohedral multilayer graphene, motivated by the recent experiment on the ABCA tetralayer showing possible spin- and valley-polarized superconductivity. They approximated the single-particle band structure by a circularly symmetric minimal model with parameters fitted by the k.p band model. Using RPA and the minimal band model, they found that p-wave superconductivity (which the authors suggested to be chiral p-wave, e.g., p+ip) can emerge with T_c varying from 100 mK to a few K, depending on the screening parameters of the Coulomb interaction. They further pointed out the topological transition within the superconducting region and argued that the results may explain the SC1 and SC2 regions in the experiment.
The subject of this manuscript is important as the new ABCA tetralayer graphene experiment may open up a new direction for realizing chiral topological superconductors and Majorana physics. Overall, the manuscript is well-written, and the qualitative results are interesting. This work shows the first microscopic calculation of the superconductivity driven by the screened Coulomb interaction using a simplified band structure. While the analysis seems appropriate at first glance, there are several outstanding issues that need to be addressed. As a result, I cannot recommend publication. I will be happy to review the manuscript again after the authors resolve all the issues. The questions/comments are as follows:
(1) The Kohn-Luttinger mechanism here (and in other graphene-based systems) seems to overestimate T_c. Unlike the phonon-mediated pairing, there is no Migdal theorem for the screened Coulomb interaction. As a result, the vertex correction and other related contributions may modify the estimated T_c significantly. The authors should discuss this issue and provide some quantitative estimates if possible.
(2) It needs to be clarified how reliable the minimal band model is based on the current results. The authors argued that ''the energy scale of trigonal warping is small in tetralayer graphene in the range of density and displacement field of interest, as evidenced by the nearly symmetric band dispersion shown in Fig. 1.'' However, it’s not evident from Fig. 1, which is a plot of E vs. k_x, that trigonal warping is indeed weak.
The k.p band structure is NOT circularly symmetric, and the dispersion along k_x and k_y (relative to the valley momentum) can be very different. The fitting in Appendix A and Fig. 5 need to be discussed more carefully. The authors may compare the density of states of the minimal model and the k.p model, which should provide some hints about the validity of the minimal model.
(3) The conclusion of chiral pairing is based on the Berry curvature argument without any quantitative calculations. I would like to know how large this splitting between two chiral order parameters is due to the effect of Berry curvature. Conventionally, one needs to check the quartic order of the order parameter in free energy to determine the chiral or nodal pairing, as shown in Ref. 19. The authors may want to check the quartic term.
(4) The authors may want to discuss other potential pairing mechanisms. What has been achieved here is that the screened Coulomb interaction may provide a way to explain the putative spin- and valley-polarized superconductivity in ABCA graphene. However, it does not rule out other possibilities. It is possible that several different pairing glues result in the experimentally observed superconductivity. Some discussions about the possible mechanisms will be useful.
Minor issues:
(5) The authors employ the Rytova-Keldysh potential, with the 2D screening length r_K as a tuning parameter, based on its inverse dependence on the band gap of multilayer graphene, and thereby on the displacement field D. On the contrary, the dual-gated Coulomb potential is considered in many other existing literature. Why did the author pick this particular one over the other one? The authors did say that the choice of the Coulomb potential (before RPA) does not affect the qualitative results. However, the should authors explain their choice when introducing the Rytova-Keldysh potential. The authors mentioned that the Rytova-Keldysh potential is often used for 2D systems of which the dielectric constant is much larger than the dielectric environment. Based on the current manuscript, it is unclear that the dielectric constant of multilayer graphene is much larger than hBN, so relevant experiments should be cited.
(6) Fig. 2(a) shows the single-particle static polarization functon(Eq. 5) by setting the frequency to zero. I have a few clarifying questions: Does Fig. 2(a) only include intraband transitions when the Fermi level aligns with the annular Fermi pocket? Are interband transitions, which are gap-dependent, effectively incorporated through the parameter r_K?
Additionally, which value of r_K is used for Fig. 2(b) and (c)? In Fig. 2(c), the attraction length scale is about 1 nm—comparable to the multilayer graphene thickness. Why, then, is the Rytova-Keldysh potential valid? The authors should clarify these points in the manuscript.
(7) In Fig. 3(c), the highest Tc is achieved at r_K = 1 nm, approximately matching the thickness of tetralayer graphene. Does using the Keldysh potential with r_K = 1 nm yield a Tc comparable to using the bare 3D Coulomb potential with RPA?
(8) According to Fig. 2(a), k_{F,2} is approximately 0.3 nm^-1, corresponding to a Fermi wavelength of around 20 nm, which greatly exceeds the 1 nm attraction length scale indicated in Fig. 2(d). How do the authors conclude that: “Our mechanism is based on the overscreening of Coulomb interaction due to charge fluctuations, which leads to an effective attraction at length scales of a few Fermi wavelengths, driving Cooper pairing.” and “The screening strongly reduces the repulsion on long length scales compared to the Fermi wavelength, and leads to an overscreening with an effective attraction at distances of a few Fermi wavelengths, as demonstrated in Fig. 2(c).”
(9) This work shows the first microscopic calculations for the screened-Coulomb-driven superconductivity in the tetralayer graphene system. However, this possibility was also suggested in Ref. [62]. The authors cited Ref. [62] in an obscure way -- They put a very short footnote [36], stating "For a mean field study of superconductivity from attraction, see Ref. [62]).'' Since the screened-Coulomb mechanism was also suggested in Ref. [62], the footnote is not accurate.
(10) Could the authors comment on the role of the WSe_2 layer in the tetralayer graphene experiment, particularly within the context of the Kohn-Luttinger mechanism and the screening effects of the Rytova-Keldysh potential?
(11) Typo in Eq. (6): The frequency omega should be zero.
(12) In the section “Topological superconductivity and Lifshitz transition”: “The quasiparticle gap ∆0 ≡ min_k Ek as a function of density n and displacement field D is shown in Fig. 4(c).” There is no Fig. 4(c).

### Reviewer 3

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

### Reviewer 4

The authors performed a calculation of a Coulomb repulsion originated theory for spin-valley polarized chiral superconductivity in tetralayer graphene, aimed at explaining the recently observed superconductivity in such systems. The theoretical calculations follow the standard mean field theory procedures and seemed to lead to desired results, and this is a timely study of the very interesting recent experiment. It is however difficult to claim how reliable the mean field calculations are for such a strongly interacting system. I also find the paper not presented clearly, with unjustified or ambiguous points in the authors calculations and arguments. I therefore cannot recommend the current paper draft to Nature Communication. My detailed questions and comments are given below.
1. The form of band dispersion in Eq. (1) is proposed in a strange way: if k_0 is fixed, the dispersion will not reach k^n (the well-known dispersion of n-layer graphene) at D=0, so D is not an independent tuning parameter. After checking App. A I can understand that k_0 and m are functions of D, and probably k_0 is proportional to D^{1/n} such that k^n dispersion can be reached at D=0. It would be more natural to redefine the first part as \sqrt{D^2+k^2/k_0^2} with k_0 roughly constant. Or at least, in the current form, the authors should explain in the main text that k_0 and m are functions of D (and k_0 proportional to D^{1/n}).
2. Related to the above question, it seems the theory proposed in this paper is largely independent of the number of graphene layers n. Are all the calculations specific for n=4, and if so, anything special about n=4? In other words, does the theory provide an understanding why the chiral superconductivity is observed in tetra-layer graphene?
3. Is the mass term m in Eq. (1) the particle-hole symmetry breaking term? Can the authors understand from their theory why the superconductivity occurs in the conduction band?
4. Some setups of the model considered are unclear. In writing down the interaction in Eq. (2) and later, are the electron operators defined for one particular spin and valley? It is difficult to find in the paper whether the pairing is intra-valley or intervalley. Also, I don’t think k_{F,1} and k_{F,2} are defined before they first appear.
5. The effective attractive interaction near r=1nm in Fig. 2(c) is counterintuitive. RPA, which can be understood as the dynamical generalization of Thomas-Fermi screening, usually only reduces the repulsion due to opposite charges accumulated nearby. It seems unlikely to have “over-screening” that the repulsion is flipped into attractions. It is more likely that the interaction is attractive in non-s wave channels, instead of being globally attractive. Although s-wave here is forbidden by spin-valley polarization, the RPA calculations seem to be independent from this assumption. Can the authors provide an intuitive picture for understanding the attraction? Also, RPA is a perturbative method for interactions much smaller than the Fermi energy, how is it justified here, where interaction is much larger than the kinetic energy (as indicated by r_s the authors calculated)?
6. A related question, is the effective RPA interaction above sufficient to induce spin-valley polarization, i.e., the starting point of the current theory? The interaction in Fig. 2(c) looks much weaker and localized than the bare interaction; the highly local interaction may resemble the Hubbard model which gives anti-ferromagnetism instead of (orbital) ferromagnetism.
7. The form factor or the interaction in Eq. (13) looks incorrect. Shouldn’t it be the inner product of u_{k+q} with u_k, and u_{k’-q} with u_{k’}?
8. I do not understand what “charge-ordered state” in the discussion mean. Does it mean Wigner Crystal? The authors may want to clarify. Also, there is (almost) no mentioning of the Lifshitz transition of Fermi surface in the main text (probably the cyan line region in Fig. 4?), which the authors should explain better.
9. The electron-phonon coupling is completely ignored in the study here. Is there a particular reason for ignoring the effect of phonons? Also, how would the authors propose to tell experimentally whether the superconductivity is from Coulomb repulsion instead of phonons? For instance, if the screening of Coulomb interaction is enhanced (by metallic gate, etc), would the authors predict an enhancement or decrease of superconducting Tc?
10. The authors only focused on the time-reversal breaking superconducting phases in the experiment. The experiment also observes more conventional superconductivity in two other parameter regimes. Do the authors have comments on the other superconductivity regimes? Is the claim that Coulomb interaction is better for realizing chiral superconductivity (in contrast to phonons which may favor s-wave superconductivity more)?
11. A minor question: I believe \omega in Eq. (6) should be set to zero already.

## Paper

## Abstract

A microscopic mechanism for chiral p-wave superconductivity from Coulomb repulsion is proposed for spin- and valley-polarized state of rhombohedral multilayer graphene. The superconducting instability arises when strong Thomas-Fermi screening of the Coulomb potential allows Friedel oscillations to take over–leading to an effective attraction on length scales below the Fermi wavelength. The superconducting critical temperature is largest at low density below a Lifshitz transition to an annular Fermi sea, where the additional pocket strongly enhances Thomas-Fermi screening. The Lifshitz transition also marks a topological phase transition from a trivial to a topological superconducting phase hosting Majorana fermions. The chirality of the superconducting order parameter is selected by the chirality of the valley-polarized Bloch electrons. Our results are in reasonable agreement with observations in a recent experiment on tetralayer graphene.

---

## Introduction

Chiral superconductivity, characterized by spontaneous time-reversal symmetry breaking and finite-angular momentum Cooper pairing1, is a long-sought quantum phase of matter with unusual superconducting and magnetic properties. Interest in chiral superconductors is further fueled by their potential for hosting topological phases and Majorana fermions2,3. While previous material candidates, such as Sr2RuO4 and UTe25–7, showed initial signs of chiral superconductivity, recent experiments strongly suggest single-component superconducting order parameters that are non-chiral8–15.

Very recently, signatures of chiral superconductivity have been observed in rhombohedral-stacked tetralayer graphene under electron doping16. While superconductivity has been previously discovered and intensively studied in crystalline trilayer17–30 and bilayer graphene31–36, the newly found superconducting state in tetralayer graphene at low density is remarkably distinctive in that it exhibits large spontaneous anomalous Hall effect above Tc and magnetic hysteresis in resistance below Tc. These observations demonstrate time-reversal-breaking superconductivity in a pure carbon system. Its pairing symmetry and pairing mechanism are open questions for investigation.

A key feature of rhombohedral multilayer graphene is the flat band dispersion near K and K0 point, leading to a strong correlation effect19,23. As a result, spin and valley isospin symmetry breaking occurs at low temperature, giving rise to half and quarter metal phases23. Interestingly, the superconducting state in tetralayer graphene at low density borders the quarter metal and its phase boundary shows no or little change with the applied magnetic field, indicating that the superconducting state is likely fully spin and valley polarized16. Thus, tetralayer graphene provides a rare opportunity for investigating Cooper pairing of single-flavor electrons in a solid-state platform.

In this work, we study the microscopic mechanism and pairing symmetry of superconductivity in multilayer graphene that develops from the spin- and valley-polarized quarter metal normal state [Fig. 1a, b]. Our mechanism is based on the overscreening of Coulomb interaction due to charge fluctuations, which leads to an effective attraction at length scales on a fraction of the Fermi wavelength, driving Cooper pairing. Using a minimal model for the band dispersion, our theory predicts that superconductivity occurs at low densities with enhanced density of states due to the annular Fermi surface and displacement field-induced flatness of the band. Based on our analysis, we further propose that a Wigner crystalline insulating state occurs at the Lifshitz transition from simply-connected to annular Fermi sea that splits the superconducting dome into two. This provides an explanation for the two proximate superconducting domes SC1 and SC2 with similar properties observed in the experiment16.

---

## Results

Band dispersion
In rhombohedral multilayer graphene, low-energy bands come from sublattice-polarized states in the top and bottom layers. An out-of-plane electric field induces a potential bias equal to 2D between these layers and opens up an energy gap while flattening the dispersion near K and K0 points. Therefore, the Fermi energy is only a few meV above the band bottom for a small electron density of around 5 × 1011 cm−2, where time-reversal-breaking superconductivity is observed.

The low-energy band dispersion is highly tunable by the electric field. As the displacement field D increases, the curvature at K and K0 changes from positive to negative19,23 as shown in Fig. 1c for ABCA tetralayer graphene, resulting in a Mexican-hat shaped dispersion. In this case, a Lifshitz transition from simply-connected to annular Fermi surface occurs when the Fermi energy crosses the top of the hat as the electron density is reduced.

We capture the essential features of the electric-field-tuned conduction band in rhombohedral n-layer graphene with a minimal band

εk = D 1 + (k/k0)2n + ℏ2k2 / 2m (1)

where D is the displacement field, k0 is a momentum scale, and m is the effective mass. The dispersion (1) is circularlysymmetric. The inclusion of additional hopping terms leads to trigonal warping. For now, we neglect trigonal warping and Berry curvature effects and will treat them perturbatively later.

Rytova-Keldysh potential
The density-density interaction can be written as

Hint = 1/2 sum_{k1,k2,q} V(q) ψ^y_{k1+q} ψ^y_{k2-q} ψ_{k2} ψ_{k1} (2)

where ψ^y_k (ψ_k) are the annihilation (creation) operators of spin-polarized electrons in a single valley. Importantly, in a 2D material surrounded by a dielectric with a lower dielectric permittivity, the Coulomb interaction between two charges can be described by the Rytova-Keldysh potential40–42, taking the form:

V(q) = e^2 / 2ϵ|q|(1 + rK|q|) (3)

where ϵ = 5ϵ0 is the dielectric permittivity of the surrounding hBN (with ϵ0 the vacuum permittivity), and rK is the Rytova-Keldysh parameter. The Rytova-Keldysh parameter depends on the difference between the dielectric response of the 2D material under study and that of the surrounding insulator. Since the 2D dielectric screening is determined by interband transitions and thereby depends on the band gap, rK of multilayer graphene is affected by the displacement field43. We will find that the superconducting pairing strength depends sensitively on rK.

Electron pairing from screened Coulomb repulsion
We study superconductivity in the spin- and valley-polarized state. This is justified because (i) valley polarization is observed to occur at a much higher temperature than superconductivity, and (ii) the primary superconducting state (SC1 in ref. 16) was observed within the quarter-metal state, and (iii) the primary superconducting states (SC1 and SC2) survive to very high in-plane magnetic fields.

Theoretically, we also expect that the energy scales of spin- and valley polarization to be much larger than superconductivity: Estimating the energy scale of isospin polarization in the Stoner model23 as Δpol ≈ ν(EF)V(2kF,2)EF ≈ 2 to 3 meV in the relevant range of density and displacement field, it is an order of magnitude larger than the pairing strength [see numerical results below].

Since total spin S2 and valley imbalance NK − NK0 are conserved quantum numbers, there are no isospin fluctuations at zero temperature that can drive superconductivity in the fully-polarized quarter metal state. This motivates us to consider a mechanism for superconductivity in the spin- and valley-polarized state based on screening of electron-electron interactions by charge fluctuations44–46. The screening is described by the charge susceptibility χRe(q,τ) = −1/A <T τ ρe,q(τ)ρe,-q(0)>, which in random phase approximation (RPA) is determined by the expression

χRe(q,iΩn)RPA = χ0e(q,iΩn) / 1 - Vq χ0e(q,iΩn) (4)

in terms of the charge susceptibility of the non-interacting electron gas

χ0e(q,iΩn) = 1/A sum_k (nF(εk) - nF(εk+q)) / (εk - εk+q + iℏΩn) (5)

where nF is the Fermi-Dirac distribution. The screened interaction potential is then

V~(q) = Vq / 1 - Vq χ0e(q,0) = Vq ϵ^-1(q,0)RPA (6)

The charge susceptibility and screened interaction potential for the annular Fermi pocket are shown in Fig. 2a, b, respectively. The q→0 limit of the denominator describing the screened interaction in Eq. (6) lim_{q→0} Vq χ0e(q,0) = e^2 / 2πℓTF defines the Thomas-Fermi screening length ℓTF = 4πϵ/e^2ν(EF).

Due to the large density of states, the charge susceptibility becomes large for momenta below twice the Fermi momentum kF,2 of the outer Fermi surface. This leads to a suppression of the electron-electron interaction at small momenta and a peak at 2kF,2. This renormalized interaction potential promotes a p-wave superconducting instability.

In real space, the screening strongly reduces the repulsion above the Thomas-Fermi screening length ℓTF. Furthermore, Friedel oscillations appear with period 2kF,1, 2kF,2 due to the two Fermi surfaces. When the Thomas-Fermi screening length is much shorter than the wavelengths π/kF,1, π/kF,2, Friedel oscillations dominate over Coulomb repulsion and lead to an effective attraction at short length scales, as obtained from our calculations shown in Fig. 2c. We find ℓTF ≈ 1 to 2 nm, for typical parameters where we observe superconductivity as discussed below, while 2π/kF,1, 2π/kF,2 is typically around 20 nm to 30 nm. This mechanism benefits from a Mexican-hat-shaped dispersion because the additional pocket contributes a large density of states, leading to a short Thomas-Fermi screening length. This enables superconductivity at a larger density.

To determine the superconducting order parameter and its critical temperature, we solve the self-consistency equations

Δ(k) = -1/A sum_{k'} V~(k-k') <ψ^y_{-k'} ψ^y_{k'}> (7)

<ψ^y_{-k} ψ^y_{k}> = - Δ(k) / 2Ek tanh(Ek / 2kBT)

where Ek is the quasiparticle energy

Ek = sqrt((εk - μ)^2 + |Δ(k)|^2) (8)

Here, the interaction V~(k-k') scatters a pair of electrons at opposite momenta (k', -k') to (k, -k).

Due to the rotational symmetry in our model, we decompose the pairing interaction into angular harmonics:

V~l(k,k') = 1/2π integral_0^{2π} dϑ e^{ilϑ} V~(ϑ,k,k') (9)

where we wrote V~(k-k') = V~(ϑ,k,k') with ϑ the angle between k and k', and k, k' the their magnitude. The order parameter can also be expanded into angular harmonics Δ(k) = sum_{l=0} ηl(k) e^{ilθ} with (kx, ky) = k(cosθ, sinθ). The equations for the critical temperature Tc for different angular harmonics decouple.

Around Tc, we linearize the self-consistency equation and find for the individual angular harmonics,

ηl(k,Tc) = - 1/8π^2 integral_0^∞ dk' k' V~l(k,k') tanh(|εk' - μ| / 2kBTc) / |εk' - μ| ηl(k',Tc) (10)

For the superconducting order parameter at zero temperature, the self-consistency relation reads

ηl(k,0) = - 1/8π^2 integral_0^∞ dk' k' V~l(k,k') ηl(k',0) / 2 sqrt((εk' - μ)^2 + |ηl(k',0)|^2) (11)

Both equations can be solved iteratively, as detailed in SM section B. This angular decomposition applies to a circularly symmetric interaction potential, where the circular symmetry is preserved for the screened potential when the dispersion is circularly symmetric.

Importantly, the screened interaction V~ is positive and large at momentum transfer q = k-k' around 2kF,2, compared to small q. Such q-dependent interaction favors an order parameter that takes opposite signs at opposite ±k points on the Fermi surface, i.e., it favors p-wave pairing.

For most superconductors, the pairing interaction is weak and therefore the pairing potential Δ(k) is small compared to the Fermi energy and only appreciable in the vicinity of the Fermi surface. For this reason, in solving the gap equation, it suffices to use “on-shell” pairing interaction V~l(k,k') at Fermi wave vectors k, k'. In contrast, in multilayer graphene, the combination of low electron density and flat band bottom leads to a larger ratio of interaction to the Fermi energy. As a consequence, we will show that Δ and Tc can be on the order of the Fermi energy. Indeed, the recent experiment on tetralayer graphene16 reports an unusually high upper critical field at low density, indicating a strong-coupling superconductor with coherence length comparable to interparticle distance. For strong-coupling superconductors, the superconducting gap Δ(k) can be large even away from the Fermi momentum. Therefore, in solving the gap equation, it is necessary to use the interaction V~l(k,k') with full k, k' dependence.

Our calculation of the density of states, ν and critical temperature Tc, as a function of electron density and displacement field, is shown in Fig. 3a, b, respectively. Both the displacement field D and the electron density n together determine the Fermi surface size and topology. For small D < Dc ≈ 40 meV, the dispersion increases monotonically with k and the Fermi surface is a single circle with kF = sqrt(4πn), whereas at large displacement field (D > Dc), a Lifshitz transition from annular to simply-connected Fermi sea occurs with increasing electron density, which is accompanied by a large jump in the normal-state density of states at the Fermi level [Fig. 3a]. Correspondingly, superconducting properties depend strongly on the displacement field. For small D, a superconducting state is found at a small density where the chemical potential lies close to the relatively flat band bottom with a large density of states. For large D, the superconducting state sets in at low densities where the Fermi sea is annular, and Tc is largest close to the Lifshitz transition.

It should be noted that the value of Tc is sensitive to the dielectric screening of Coulomb repulsion by the multilayer graphene, which, in turn, depends on the displacement field-induced band gap. As a function of the Rytova-Keldysh parameter rK [Fig. 3c], the typical Tc at D = 60 meV ranges from Tc ≈ 3 K at rK = 1 nm to a suppression of Tc to below 0.1 K above rK = 10 nm. With bare Coulomb repulsion, a maximal Tc ≈ 8 K is obtained, see SM section H. The decrease of Tc with strong dielectric screening is consistent with electron pairing by Coulomb repulsion. Without knowing the value of rK for tetralayer graphene, we cannot make a quantitative prediction of Tc. Nonetheless, for the reasonable range of rK considered here, superconductivity always onsets at n < 0.7 × 1012 cm−2 in agreement with experimental observation, and the calculated Tc is acceptable compared to the experimental value, especially considering that the mean-field theory generally predicts higher values of Tc.

Going beyond our mean-field treatment, we estimate the critical temperature for a BKT transition47–49 kBTBKT = π/2 J determined by the superfluid stiffness. An order-of-magnitude estimate is obtained using the superfluid stiffness expression J = ℏ^2n/4m for a quadratic band whose mass m ≈ 2me is matched so that its density of states matches the typical density of state ν(EF) ≈ 2νe at the Fermi energy of our model [compare Fig. 3a]. Based on this estimate, we find a typical BKT transition temperature kBTBKT ≈ 0.9 K at n = 0.5 × 1012 cm−2. This indicates that the critical temperature in this system may be limited by vortex proliferation in the BKT transition.

Strong-coupling superconductivity
For the chiral px ± ipy pairing, the calculated pairing potential Δ(k) at T = 0 can reach a few tenths of the Fermi energy. Notably, Δ(k) is large not only close to the Fermi surface, but also extends to several times the Fermi wavevector with a sign change at around 2kF,2 [Fig. 4a]. Its functional form closely follows the interaction potential up to a proportionality factor setting the pairing strength [see SM section C]. The presence of substantial pairing potential away from the Fermi surfaces is a consequence of the strong-coupling nature of this superconducting state—because kBTc and Δ are of the order of the Fermi energy, pairing between electrons away from the Fermi surface is relevant. This is captured by our direct solution of Eqs. (10), (11).

Due to the large pairing potential, the chemical potential changes appreciably in the superconducting state. This can be estimated by taking into account the pairing potential in relating electron density to chemical potential

n = 1/2πℏ^2 integral d^2k (1 - (εk - μ) / Ek) (12)

At zero temperature, the change in chemical potential approaches 0.1 meV. The change in electron density is taken into account in Fig. 3a. The change in chemical potential δμ ∝ |Δ|^2 is expected to increase linearly with decreasing temperature.

Topological superconductivity and Lifshitz transition
The quasiparticle gap Δ0 = min_k Ek as a function of density n and displacement field D is shown in Fig. 4b. Our p±ip superconductor generally has a full gap, except at the Lifshitz transition from simply-connected to annular Fermi sea, where the system has a point node at the Fermi point k = 0 at which the pairing potential vanishes. The closing of the quasiparticle gap marks a topological quantum phase transition from a topological superconductor with unity Chern number in the region with a single Fermi pocket to a topologically trivial state in the annular region at large displacement fields50,51. The topological superconductor at small displacement fields hosts chiral Majorana edge modes and Majorana zero modes in the vortex2. In contrast, the trivial state with annular Fermi sea is adiabatically connected to the Bose-Einstein limit μ → −∞, because the pairing potential Δ(k) is finite at the band bottom of the Mexican hat dispersion, which forms a ring at k ≠ 0. Note that in our theory, even though the superconducting gap vanishes at k = 0 at the Lifshitz transition, the gap at the outer Fermi surface Δ(kF2) and critical temperature remains large throughout the transition – therefore the quasiparticle gap closure is not visible in the critical temperature calculations Fig. 3b.

Competing state
Since the p-wave superconductivity found in our RPA calculation occurs at relatively low density, it is important to consider its competition with the Wigner crystal state, which generally appears in 2D Coulomb systems at sufficiently low density. To estimate the transition to the Wigner crystal, we compute the gas parameter rs = Eint/Ekin given by the ratio of interaction Eint to kinetic energy Ekin52. In our calculations, we find that the superconducting state is robust against the Wigner crystal state for rs < 40. The transition to the Wigner crystal depends sensitively on the gate screening as the interparticle distances at low density approach tens of nm.

In Fig. 4, the region where rs > 40 is encircled by the cyan line; in a homogeneous electron gas, the transition to a Wigner crystal occurs around rs ≈ 30–4052–56. This region is where the band bottom is most flat, so that the kinetic energy per particle is low. It coincides with the region where the density of states is largest, see Fig. 3a. We expect crystalline order is likely to dominate there, so that the superconducting region is divided into two, separated by an insulating Wigner crystal state.

Trigonal warping and Berry curvature effects
Our minimal model neglects trigonal warping, which arises from electron hoppings beyond nearest-neighbor atoms in multilayer graphene. With trigonal warping, the band dispersion becomes asymmetric εk ≠ ε-k, which weakens intravalley pairing between ±k states. Fortunately, the energy scale of trigonal warping is small in tetralayer graphene in the range of density and displacement field of interest, as evidenced by the nearly symmetric band dispersion in Fig. 1. For the range of parameters where we observe superconductivity, the pairing is driven by the interaction energy, and therefore is robust against the pair breaking effect of trigonal warping.

Up to now, we have neglected the effect of electron Bloch wave functions |uk> within the unit cell. The momentum dependence of the complex-valued wavefunction |uk> gives rise to Berry curvature, which in the presence of time-reversal symmetry breaking, leads to an orbital magnetic moment in the polarized valley57. We have shown that the chirality of the Bloch wave functions is responsible for the chirality of the superconducting order parameter. We also verified that our mechanism strongly favors p-wave pairing over higher angular momenta, see SM section G.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

In this paper, the authors propose chiral p-wave superconductivity in tetralayer graphene. Considering a quarter metal state with a nearly flat band, they obtain a chiral p-wave superconducting state from the screened Coulomb interaction. They also find the Fermi surface of the system shows the Lifshitz transition, which results in a topological phase transition. The topic is timely, and the result is interesting. However, the following points need to be clarified before making a recommendation, as they are crucial for understanding and accepting the research.
1. The authors only consider a particular multilayer graphene, ABCA tetralayer graphene. The author should clarify why they chose this specific multilayer graphene. For example, is it possible to obtain a similar result in trilayer graphene or differently stacked graphene
2. The authors assume a spin and magnetic gap deriving the quarter metal, then calculate the superconducting critical temperature independently from a screened Coulomb interaction. However, the magnetic order itself also originates from the Coulomb interaction. The author should justify this treatment.
3. A minor point: When D is introduced in the left column on page 2 for the first time, the author should explicitly mention its definition because 2D is often used to represent “two dimensions.”

### Reviewer 2

The authors proposed that the screened Coulomb interaction can realize chiral superconductivity in rhombohedral multilayer graphene, motivated by the recent experiment on the ABCA tetralayer showing possible spin- and valley-polarized superconductivity. They approximated the single-particle band structure by a circularly symmetric minimal model with parameters fitted by the k.p band model. Using RPA and the minimal band model, they found that p-wave superconductivity (which the authors suggested to be chiral p-wave, e.g., p+ip) can emerge with T_c varying from 100 mK to a few K, depending on the screening parameters of the Coulomb interaction. They further pointed out the topological transition within the superconducting region and argued that the results may explain the SC1 and SC2 regions in the experiment.
The subject of this manuscript is important as the new ABCA tetralayer graphene experiment may open up a new direction for realizing chiral topological superconductors and Majorana physics. Overall, the manuscript is well-written, and the qualitative results are interesting. This work shows the first microscopic calculation of the superconductivity driven by the screened Coulomb interaction using a simplified band structure. While the analysis seems appropriate at first glance, there are several outstanding issues that need to be addressed. As a result, I cannot recommend publication. I will be happy to review the manuscript again after the authors resolve all the issues. The questions/comments are as follows:
(1) The Kohn-Luttinger mechanism here (and in other graphene-based systems) seems to overestimate T_c. Unlike the phonon-mediated pairing, there is no Migdal theorem for the screened Coulomb interaction. As a result, the vertex correction and other related contributions may modify the estimated T_c significantly. The authors should discuss this issue and provide some quantitative estimates if possible.
(2) It needs to be clarified how reliable the minimal band model is based on the current results. The authors argued that ''the energy scale of trigonal warping is small in tetralayer graphene in the range of density and displacement field of interest, as evidenced by the nearly symmetric band dispersion shown in Fig. 1.'' However, it’s not evident from Fig. 1, which is a plot of E vs. k_x, that trigonal warping is indeed weak.
The k.p band structure is NOT circularly symmetric, and the dispersion along k_x and k_y (relative to the valley momentum) can be very different. The fitting in Appendix A and Fig. 5 need to be discussed more carefully. The authors may compare the density of states of the minimal model and the k.p model, which should provide some hints about the validity of the minimal model.
(3) The conclusion of chiral pairing is based on the Berry curvature argument without any quantitative calculations. I would like to know how large this splitting between two chiral order parameters is due to the effect of Berry curvature. Conventionally, one needs to check the quartic order of the order parameter in free energy to determine the chiral or nodal pairing, as shown in Ref. 19. The authors may want to check the quartic term.
(4) The authors may want to discuss other potential pairing mechanisms. What has been achieved here is that the screened Coulomb interaction may provide a way to explain the putative spin- and valley-polarized superconductivity in ABCA graphene. However, it does not rule out other possibilities. It is possible that several different pairing glues result in the experimentally observed superconductivity. Some discussions about the possible mechanisms will be useful.
Minor issues:
(5) The authors employ the Rytova-Keldysh potential, with the 2D screening length r_K as a tuning parameter, based on its inverse dependence on the band gap of multilayer graphene, and thereby on the displacement field D. On the contrary, the dual-gated Coulomb potential is considered in many other existing literature. Why did the author pick this particular one over the other one? The authors did say that the choice of the Coulomb potential (before RPA) does not affect the qualitative results. However, the should authors explain their choice when introducing the Rytova-Keldysh potential. The authors mentioned that the Rytova-Keldysh potential is often used for 2D systems of which the dielectric constant is much larger than the dielectric environment. Based on the current manuscript, it is unclear that the dielectric constant of multilayer graphene is much larger than hBN, so relevant experiments should be cited.
(6) Fig. 2(a) shows the single-particle static polarization functon(Eq. 5) by setting the frequency to zero. I have a few clarifying questions: Does Fig. 2(a) only include intraband transitions when the Fermi level aligns with the annular Fermi pocket? Are interband transitions, which are gap-dependent, effectively incorporated through the parameter r_K?
Additionally, which value of r_K is used for Fig. 2(b) and (c)? In Fig. 2(c), the attraction length scale is about 1 nm—comparable to the multilayer graphene thickness. Why, then, is the Rytova-Keldysh potential valid? The authors should clarify these points in the manuscript.
(7) In Fig. 3(c), the highest Tc is achieved at r_K = 1 nm, approximately matching the thickness of tetralayer graphene. Does using the Keldysh potential with r_K = 1 nm yield a Tc comparable to using the bare 3D Coulomb potential with RPA?
(8) According to Fig. 2(a), k_{F,2} is approximately 0.3 nm^-1, corresponding to a Fermi wavelength of around 20 nm, which greatly exceeds the 1 nm attraction length scale indicated in Fig. 2(d). How do the authors conclude that: “Our mechanism is based on the overscreening of Coulomb interaction due to charge fluctuations, which leads to an effective attraction at length scales of a few Fermi wavelengths, driving Cooper pairing.” and “The screening strongly reduces the repulsion on long length scales compared to the Fermi wavelength, and leads to an overscreening with an effective attraction at distances of a few Fermi wavelengths, as demonstrated in Fig. 2(c).”
(9) This work shows the first microscopic calculations for the screened-Coulomb-driven superconductivity in the tetralayer graphene system. However, this possibility was also suggested in Ref. [62]. The authors cited Ref. [62] in an obscure way -- They put a very short footnote [36], stating "For a mean field study of superconductivity from attraction, see Ref. [62]).'' Since the screened-Coulomb mechanism was also suggested in Ref. [62], the footnote is not accurate.
(10) Could the authors comment on the role of the WSe_2 layer in the tetralayer graphene experiment, particularly within the context of the Kohn-Luttinger mechanism and the screening effects of the Rytova-Keldysh potential?
(11) Typo in Eq. (6): The frequency omega should be zero.
(12) In the section “Topological superconductivity and Lifshitz transition”: “The quasiparticle gap ∆0 ≡ min_k Ek as a function of density n and displacement field D is shown in Fig. 4(c).” There is no Fig. 4(c).
